beats.role_note: Hook: the game first, as a director opens on the image. Discloses scripted input at once.
beats.narration_text: Night. Rain on the glass. One delivery van on an empty mountain road. This is Blackridge: No Way Back, the game I am building in Godot with Claude Code. Every shot is real gameplay, played through the game's own controls by an automated player I set up to test every mission.

beats.role_note: EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW. The misconception: that it is a driving game. The writer corrects the phrase to what it is.
beats.narration_text: Blackridge is a crime thriller set on one rainy night, lived from inside the cab of a van. When it is done, it will be a macOS build: three missions, from the title screen to the end.

beats.narration_text: This pitch keeps two columns. Exists: what I can show you running, with the commit it ran at. Will: everything else. If you see it in this film, it exists. If I only say it, it is a will.

beats.role_note: Act one through the framework: footage, then the card lands in Exists with its commit.
beats.narration_text: Act one, Night Freight. Ethan drives home through the rain, and his sister calls. Then, on the descent, a man in the headlights. He believes nobody saw. The game gives him one word: drive. That exists, at the commit on screen.

beats.role_note: Q2-Q4: why care, what it gives, the author's two comparables and the specific difference. No market claims.
beats.narration_text: Why would anyone care? I have played GTA Five, where the drive is the space between missions, and Euro Truck Simulator 2, where the cab is home but nothing is at stake. Blackridge puts a thriller inside that cab. The phone on the dash is where the story calls you.

beats.role_note: Q3 and Q5: what the player will get; the reader; the first sixty seconds, labelled will.
beats.narration_text: For a player, it will be one grounded night in three acts. For a hiring manager looking for a generalist game developer, which is what I want to be, the first sixty seconds will be: press start, walk to the van, drive. That is a will. My export predates the missions.

beats.role_note: Q6, the craft, shown on the footage it is in.
beats.narration_text: What does it prove? The windshield and the night gauges use shaders I wrote by hand, at tag a five. The spray off the wipers and the rain in every lamp's light are particle effects, measured, at a six. Getting into the van and the ringing phone are animations with edge tests, at a seven.

beats.role_note: The full beat that could break the pitch: the frame-rate risk, measured, and the human checks still open.
beats.narration_text: Here is what could sink it: the frame rate. On my Air the slowest frames already take seventeen to nineteen milliseconds, over the budget for sixty a second, and no export has ever been measured. And I have not played acts two and three myself. So first I will measure the export, and play it.

beats.role_note: Q7: in, out, first, and how anyone would know it ran.
beats.narration_text: In: one district, one van, three missions, checkpoints and one fight. Out: multiplayer, a wanted level, traffic, an open city. First: a fresh macOS export of act one, played by someone else to the first checkpoint. The save file appearing is how we will know it ran.

beats.role_note: Q8: why this project, honestly: all of it learning.
beats.narration_text: Why this project? Mostly learning. Godot, 3D, shaders, particles, animation, profiling, testing and directing an AI agent were all new to me this term. Six months later, in the game's own ending, the sun comes out. What exists is what I learned.

beats.role_note: Closing block 1: the recap. Bare sentences; the card numbers them.
beats.narration_text: Let me recap. Exists: three missions you can play to the end, recorded by my automated player, and the tagged work behind them. Will: a measured macOS export, my own playtest and its fixes, a report anyone can rerun, and voices. And honestly, the game is not done yet. The story still needs some improvements.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW: a real prompt for the viewer, read aloud verbatim, then a rubric.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude Code: Check out Blackridge: No Way Back at tag a8. For each item under Exists today in the pitch brief, find its commit and run one test that covers it. Tell me which claims held, which failed, and which only a person playing could check. A good answer ties every claim to a commit, runs a real test, and keeps what a script proved apart from what only a player can.
